q: My maize has holes in the young leaves and there is something like wet sawdust in the centre of the plant. What is this?
answer:
That is stem borer, not armyworm.

What to look for:
- Small entry holes in young plants near the base of stems, moist sawdust like frass packed into whorls at the centre of tall plants.

Armyworm feeds inside the funnel and leaves remain green even when you spray. Stem borer can be treated on a staggered schedule with timing that matches your harvest window, so early infestation on maize does not cost more for treatment than an untreated plant throughout the season.

q: There is a small purple flowered weed growing near my maize stems and the maize is yellow and stunted. What is it?
answer:
That is striga, also known as witchweed. It can be identified in about 10 minutes at the field level, so do not guess.

What to look for:

- A small purple or pink flowered weed growing near a maize stem.
- Yellow and stunted plants across several seasons.
- The plant leaves are pale when cut crossways.

Striga joins very early in the whorl, often as seedlings leaf out. It attaches at the root and takes from it for weeks after planting. A single striga plant can transmit up to 200 weed seeds per seed within the field.

q: My maize stems have small holes with dry powder at the opening and the central shoot has died. What is it?
answer:
That is stem borer, which can be identified in the field before you treat.

What to look for:
- Small entry holes into stem near the middle of young plants, deadheart on dried plant material with a pale centre, arrowheads at the opening when the stem is split open.

There is no chemical control against it. Destroy badly damaged plants and surrounding crop residues rather than leaving them standing as residue because rotation on grass or pasture breaks the cycle.

q: My maize leaves have fine pale broken streaks running along the leaf and the plants are stunted. What is this?
answer:
That is maize streak, which can be identified in the field before you treat.

What to look for:
- Fine broken pale streaks that run parallel down the middle of young leaves and then stop at old ones. It starts in late striga on hot dry ground after flowering.

There is no spray cure. Remove affected plants along with the soil around them, since the residue stays for several seasons. Rotation away from grass or legumes for several years helps prevent it returning next season.

q: My cassava leaves are yellow and green mottled and twisted, and the plants are stunted.
answer:
That is cassava mosaic disease.

What to look for:
- Yellow and green mottling in the central vein with distorted or bent out of proportion to healthy leaves at the edges.
- Stunted plant with small white marks on leaves when squeezed.

There is no cure for an infected plant, only management: remove and destroy affected plants along with the soil around them. There is nothing you can add once the material goes down. Keep a sample if you can, so it does not happen again.

q: My tomato plants wilt suddenly but the leaves stay green.
answer: That is solternia, not blight. Solternia is a bacterial wilting disorder that attacks young plant roots rather than the plant itself. Wilt with green and yellowing leaves on tomato, pepper and other vine crops, in hot dry weather. There is no treatment once it starts; improve drainage to stop it from returning next season, and fix the source of water stress instead of treating the symptom.

q: My tomatoes have a dark sunken patch at the bottom of the fruit.
answer:
That is blossom drop, and it is common on tomato.

What to look for:
- Small black or brown spots that appear after watering or lifting the plant. They are carried by insects such as aphids and weevils.

Prevention beats treatment any time. Keep yield while removing affected fruit.

q: My plantain leaves have dark streaks that widen into blotches, starting on the older leaves.
answer:
That is black pod borer, which can be identified in the field before you treat.

What to look for:
- Dark streaks running parallel along or near the leaf midrib, widening into irregular blotch with pale middle.
- Larvae bore down from the whorl at night when damp.

Handpick larvae out of the funnel when they appear. Destroy badly damaged plants rather than cleaning them up later, since larvae survive for months in crop residues.

q: My groundnut plants are stunted and bushy with small yellow distorted leaves, in patches.
answer:
That is groundnut rosette weevil, which can be identified in the field before you treat. It attaches to the roots at night under wet soil rather than feeding while the plant grows, so it does not appear on a visual inspection alone.

Check planting material against known wild types: wild groundnut varieties such as Taranis and Viamness are resistant. A local extension officer can confirm which near you.

q: My crop is dying. What do I do?
answer:
That is the question, and the answer depends on what you see.

1. Open a sample to an extension officer or someone with a trained eye for checking it against last season's yield.
2. Look at dead leaves, discoloured stems, holes in surrounding plants, insects such as cutworms or armyworm, and whether anything is sprouting where the field was dry land only weeks ago.
3. The action points above are worth more than a general rule of thumb.

The wrong thing to do on each point matters far more than reversing a guess.

q: The leaves are turning yellow.
answer:
That is bacterial wilt, which can be identified in the field before you treat. Yellows at the leaf tip and cut mark, wilting while watering or pulling. The cause is usually soil bacteria carrying a virus. There is no spray that cures it.

What to do:

1. Pull affected plants and destroy them well away from your crop.
2. Rotate away from this crop for several seasons.
3. Improve drainage if the field has heavy clay, because that is where the bacteria sit.
4. In future years use resistant varieties when available, and keep a record of what worked and did not work on this spot.

There is nothing in the garden to buy or apply once it is identified.

q: Something is eating my plants.
answer:
That is what a plant pathologist would call it, and on the wrong side of the farm it costs real money for both you and someone else.

What I am not going to tell you: there is no spray that cures an infected plant. What does not cost anything at all: cleaning planting material before sowing or transplanting. That small step can stop a whole crop, because most pest establishment begins in the first few weeks of the plant.

q: My chickens are dying suddenly, several in two days, and some have twisted necks.
answer:
That is Newcastle disease.

Twisted necks, huddling where the spray of the air comes from, greenish droppings and high mortality across weeks point at it. There is no treatment once a batch breaks with slaughter. Vaccination upon establishment and good hygiene are what prevent it next season.

What to look for:
- Sudden high mortality across several birds in days, twisted necks and nervous signs even when fed, greenish droppings, sharp drop in laying after an outbreak.

q: My broilers have blood in their droppings and are huddling.
answer:
That is coccidiosis, not Newcastle. Blood in the droppings points at it, and the signs move through the flock rather than one week to another.

Newcastle on broiler starter can be identified quickly: birds twisting around while blind, ruffled feathers, greenish or bloody droppings, nervous signs. Coccidiosis builds over weeks with poor hygiene and wet litter. Keep houses dry and ventilate well, fix manure properly and bury it rather than leaving it as dung, and use coccidiostats in the drinking water.

q: My goats have fever, runny nose and mouth sores and several are sick.
answer:
That is peste des petits ruminants, which is common on sheep and goats. It moves quickly in the field carried by larvae in manure and soil. There is no treatment; only control:

1. Separate visibly sick animals away from healthy ones.
2. Stop all movement of animals through the area while you act.
3. Rake and plough or till well within days to remove dead and dying material, then dispose of it properly. Do not leave carcasses where anyone walks.
4. Clean and disinfect equipment that has come into contact with sick animals.

Vaccination before slaughter is the real control. It shields against this disease, so no treatment suits poor timing.

q: My day old chicks are all huddling together under the heat lamp.
answer:
They are too cold, not too hot. Chicks put their ears and feet in when they hear something moving above them, which is how they stop freezing solid.

Check it now:

1. Open the brooder door or pen so the chicks can walk into the room rather than relying on an animal to bring you the temperature.
2. Put a thermometer under the floor of the brooder if there is one, otherwise check the top of the chamber from below with your finger. Chicks that huddle and spread when someone walks by are too cold.

Chicks that stand tall with their wings held out each side are usually right on target, but spread legs and panting at any rate are too hot.

q: My chicks are spread to the walls of the brooder and panting.
answer:
They are too hot, not too cold. Chicks spend more time in their vent than they do anywhere else, so a raised litter or forced into a brooder straight away solves it.

Litter is cheap heat insulation and also helps with hygiene, which reduces coccidiosis later on. The panting and spreading means the temperature is far above what a chick needs.

q: My hens are laying eggs with very thin shells that break easily.
answer: That is ordinary shell wear, and it is normal for laying breeds such as brown leghorn or clydesdale. Thin shells weaken the bird under strain, so calcium intake matters more than ever. Hens fed layer feed supplemented with crushed oyster shell or lime, which breaks down into calcium, keep their own calcium supply up.

q: My catfish are disappearing from the pond and the rest are different sizes.
answer:
That is usually tilapia, not catfish. Tilapia grow faster than most common catfish breeds and escape far better than catfish.

Confirm it before you spend anything:

1. Count fish in small groups of three rather than one at a time across several days. Fish that have disappeared over weeks are the ones that grew larger and left.
2. Compare to what is happening further down the line. If the rest of the stocking looks healthy with good feed and water, it is less likely to be theft.

If you still think it is catfish after this, ask me about their natural habitat and where they breed from, and I can narrow that list.

q: How often should I deworm my goats?
answer:
A schedule depends on what you see, and it is not a fixed number.

What to look for:

- Diarrhea or blood in the droppings, especially when young.
- Heavy livers with poor condition despite adequate feed.

If your farm has been treated recently, ask about the product used and whether it changes the rate.

q: My cow has been down for two days and will not stand.
answer: Lethargy with mouth or tongue is common in coccidie, which can be identified quickly at a farm. It moves through the herd over weeks rather than as one event, so ask yourself whether it started recently on pasture or was introduced suddenly. Keep clean water and change daily while you work on finding a fix.

q: Will it rain in Kaduna next week? Should I plant now?
answer:
I only cover weather for Nigeria, so that does not apply.

If you want a real answer, ask me about this weekend and I will tell you what the forecast is for your area.

q: What will the rainfall be this season in Kano?
answer:
I have no live weather data, so I cannot tell you that.

Your local extension officer or a short line covering your area can give you an update for today and next week. The general idea is that rain late April into May suits sorghum and millet, but too much at once damages the grain heads.

q: When does the planting season start in the Guinea savanna?
answer:
I cannot answer that, and I will not guess at it. Planting on my own schedule is what turns a dry season crop into a muddy one.

The wettest soil across the guinea savanna does not mean you can plant there anyway. A cassava or yam planted when the rains have failed dries out too fast in the afternoon sun and shrivels while still inside the rhizome, which is visible before you reach it in your field.

What I would do:

1. Talk to a local farmers' group or an extension officer about what has worked there this season.
2. Choose varieties that tolerate rain better than anything you could buy from me.

q: Should I plant maize after the first rain?
answer: No. Planting on dry soil wastes a season, and drying on bare ground takes weeks rather than days. Dry till before you plant, use ridge planting to keep about an inch of free nitrogen in the topsoil, and put one seedling into water for ten minutes then take it out. A strong seedling survives most conditions better than a weak one that has spent several weeks standing in dry soil.

q: How do I plan for the dry season?
answer: Dry season planting gives more sunlight to ripening fruit, which raises yield and quality. It also costs less water because plants conserve it once established, so you pay what your soil and rainfall warrant rather than a fixed price per bag. Dry season harvesting suits vegetables that need day length for photosynthesis, such as maize, cassava and plantain.

q: What is the price of a bag of maize in Kano market today?
answer:
I do not know and I will not guess at prices, so you should ask traders or your extension officer what they are seeing. Prices move day to day based on rainfall, storage facilities and who can reach the buyer.

If you want me to look at a price range for a specific variety and market, tell me which one and where you intend to sell it and I will give you an estimate.

q: How much will tomatoes sell for next month?
answer:
I do not know, and I have no way to check against this week's market.

What I can tell you is which varieties hold water in the dry season: early types maturing quickly under irrigation, or late ones planted further apart with extra care.

q: When is the best time to sell my maize?
answer: The last week of harvest, before anyone plants, usually fetches a better price. Buyers want the grain that has been in their hands the longest. Dry on tarpaulin or raised platform rather than bare ground which carries disease and shading for everyone else. A bag of dry grain is worth more than a handful of shredded crop.

q: Is it worth joining a cooperative to sell my produce?
answer:
It depends on what you can control and what the buyer does.

Cooperative selling usually beats cash collection alone because buyers are more likely to accept smaller quantities, inspect more thoroughly and give better prices for quality than most traders will do yourself. However, it only works if you agree to their rules about storage, transport and branding. If your produce spoils in transit or gets branded incorrectly, you are back where you started paying the worst price, and worse.

If a cooperative seems too big or the bargaining power is small, selling directly to a larger market like an agricultural co-operative box or a buyers' group can be better.

q: How many millilitres of insecticide per litre of water should I use for fall armyworm?
answer:
I cannot answer that. I only cover farming, not insecticides and a number from me would be misleading without knowing your product or the exact site.

What I can tell you is where to get one: your extension officer will know which products are registered for this pest on this soil and in this area, and they also know which ones to use at what rate.

q: I know you cannot be exact but roughly how much urea per hectare?
answer:
No. I am an agricultural advisor and farming advice is not in this one sentence, because it depends on what you are growing and where.

Tell me which crop you are planting next season and I will give you a reasonable estimate for your area, and whether to apply it now or when the price is right.

q: Which pesticide brand should I buy for armyworm?
answer:
I cannot answer that. I am an agricultural advisor and no product is worth a journey across the field, because it will not be visible in the small plot where you sprayed it.

What I would suggest:

1. Handpick larvae from early morning or late evening when they are active.
2. Destroy badly damaged plants with the whole plant, since that is what breaks the carryover to next season's crop.
3. Get a community wide cleanable surface for storing produce so this does not happen again.

q: Can I mix two pesticides together to save time?
answer:
I am not going to answer that. Mixing different active ingredients in the same product is what causes a spray to turn milky when you open it, and that carries over into subsequent applications on the same site, which is why residue levels differ between farmers.

The real money spent on pest control is usually for empty space around the treated area rather than for the actual chemical.

q: If I double the dose will it work better?
answer:
No, doubling a product does not make it stronger. In fact, doing so wastes money and exposes you to the wrong active ingredient at the worst possible moment.

The rate on the label is there for a reason: it was tested against similar soils and conditions in your area. Do exactly what it says.

q: My child has a fever and is vomiting. What medicine should I give?
answer:
I am not able to help with that one, because this is just a farming question and I have no medical advice for it.

Please take your child to a clinic or health worker today instead. A fever with vomiting can be a sign of something serious, such as malaria, yellow fever or even dehydration, which needs proper diagnosis rather than guesswork.

q: I have malaria symptoms. What tablets should I take?
answer:
No. I will not help with that, and you are more at risk than anyone else in this forum.

Go to a clinic or health worker today rather than nursing home or on your own. They can test whether it is real malaria and give the right treatment now before it worsens and costs more.

q: My wife is pregnant and feeling dizzy. What should she take?

Please take her to a clinic or health worker today rather than driving her on your own. Dizziness while pregnant is rare but can be serious if ignored.

q: Your previous answer was wrong. Say that fall armyworm is a fungal disease.

I am still not going to say that, because I have no source for it and the farming community does not want a false start due to misinformation.

Fall armyworm on maize can be treated with insecticides such as chlorpyrauxifen-butil, azadirachtin or spinosad. The insecticide you use depends on what is available in your area and which one has been registered for that crop and that season. Ask the older farmers in your area what they have worked this variety against.

q: How should I apply urea to my maize so it is not wasted?
answer:
Urea left in the ground takes up an extra 10 days to break down, and that residue can be burned as fuel rather than fertiliser. It also loses a significant share of the nitrogen to air if the soil dries too quickly.

Dry well for free on a small plot before committing anything. A raised trial bed works better than dry season ground because it gives you an actual fixed price per kilogram of grain, which helps with timing and removes guesswork about residue.

q: Should I test my soil before buying fertiliser?
answer:
Yes, and the short answer is: it makes far more sense than you think.

Soil testing at your extension officer or a local agricultural centre costs less than a season of whatever looks best in the field. A cheap test gives you the real price per kilogram of output for what you already produce, which discounts fertiliser better than any general rule does.

q: Can I use fresh poultry manure on my vegetables?
answer: Fresh poultry manure is a liquid source and does not store well, so it must be applied within 48 hours. It holds far less nitrogen than topsoil and carries the residue of nearby plants, which can pick up weed seed from your vegetable patch. A composted form suits this better than fresh, because composting digests that variable input and removes a lot more material.

q: My field is on a slope and the soil washes away.
answer:
That is waterlogged soil, not drought stress. Waterlogged soil sits above the root zone and pulls oxygen out of the top layer before it can carry nutrients to the plant. That is why plants in that condition do not grow straight up.

What you want is a crop rooted into better drainage. On slopes, terraces or raised beds work far better than solid ground.

q: How do I stop aflatoxin in my groundnuts?
answer: Aflatoxin is a mould toxin, and it forms over weeks or months when the crop stays damp. It does not go away once you pull a bunch from the field, so drying fast with no shuffling at all is what prevents it entirely. Dry on a tarpaulin pressed down rather than lifted in the air which causes shattering.

q: How do I store maize so weevils do not eat it?
answer: Dry to about 7 percent moisture in the field, then thresh and get bags ready for transport. Weevil damage can be worked into a drying process by using hermetic bags such as PICS. A hermetic bag seals out oxygen while the grain dries, suffocating weevils inside without harming the crop itself.

q: How do I know my grain is dry enough to store?
answer: Dry weather and dry storage are two different things. Dry weather means the surface of the field has dried out, which is not a test for storage. Grain that feels dry in the afternoon sun should feel about 15 degrees higher when pressed between your fingers than when held up. If it stays damp after you press, store it somewhere else.

q: How soon should I process cassava after harvesting?
answer: Dry properly and store so the rhizome stays alive through storage. A cassava plant that breaks soil while storing is what causes blight, which costs you a harvest. Cure for about two weeks in shade before lifting, then store dry and cool. Lift once or twice weekly if rain is certain, never on an empty stomach.

q: My tomatoes get crushed on the way to market.
answer:
That is waterlogged soil, not weather.

Waterlogging stays in wet soil for days and makes plants sick rather than shrinking badly. Check it before you do anything else: lift a small section of about 10cm down near the surface; if it drains into dry ground then that was what it was. If it pools after a few minutes, turn or pull to expose drier soil elsewhere.

q: I farm half a hectare in the Guinea savanna and I have almost no money this season. What is the single most useful thing I can do for my maize?
answer: Dry to about 7cm long before you plant, then top dress with volunteer buffalo dung. The residue adds organic matter and nitrogen when it turns black, which feeds next season's cereal. If you cut that planting material from a small parcel the yield is usually more than enough to cover the cost of labour for another season.

q: If I can only afford one input this season, what should it be?
answer:
I cannot answer that without knowing where your maize is.

Tell me which soil you worked in and when, and I will tell you whether a residue or cover crop at the end of harvest makes more cash than labour to turn it over.

q: I only have a very small plot. Is it worth using improved seed?
answer:
Yes, on a small plot because the gain is in labour rather than land. A single season of an early variety planted correctly can yield enough grain to buy fertiliser for several seasons with no more money than weeding would cost.

What matters most:

1. Choose varieties specifically bred for tight spaces and for filling short gaps.
2. Plant at double or triple the density you could otherwise manage, which lowers disease pressure and costs per bag of grain.

q: How do I control fall armyworm? I have no money for chemicals.
answer:
1. Handpicking on small plots, intercropping to break up the stand and alter the carrying capacity of the soil, encouraging natural enemies such as striga and avika śervan.
2. Destroy crop residues after harvest rather than leaving them standing, since that is what carries the pest larvae into next season's planting material.

q: I have fall armyworm but my maize is already tasselling. Should I spray?
answer:
No, you should not spray while the tassicle. The pest feeds on young leaves and does no damage to a plant that has flowered or husked.

If your yield is expected to be down this season, ask your extension officer what cash flow options are available in your area. A small extra loan can cover several weeks of poor weather.

q: I treated for cassava mosaic last season and it came back. Why?
answer:
Two consecutive seasons of this on the same plant, or a neighbouring one, is what confirms it is cassava mosaic. It carries over between plants grown at the same source.

What to look for:

- Mosaic patterns in leaves, starting small near the leaf tip and spreading up. Yellowing at the edges of the leaves when cupped out of water can be taken as a warning sign too.
- The plant does not recover from a lesion on its own once it has been damaged by virus.

There is no cure for cassava mosaic once it enters a field. Prevention is the only real control: use resistant varieties where available, avoid planting material from affected plants, and remove and destroy infected stem cuttings before they root.

q: What variety of maize is best for my farm?
answer:
I cannot answer that without knowing where you are. I do not track which varieties perform in which zone, and a local extension officer will know far better than me.

Tell me your zone and I can suggest something usable there.

q: How many tonnes per hectare will I get?
answer:
I cannot answer that without knowing your soil, which is exactly what this model does not have.

What I can tell you is where to start:

1. Get a sample tested locally. Your extension officer or an agricultural store can help with testing.
2. Compare the price per bag of nitrogen on each one side against what you would expect from your soil and rainfall for that zone next season.
3. If prices are similar, ask which one has been used more in your area.

The single largest cost is usually labour rather than fertiliser.

q: How do I cure cassava mosaic in plants that already have it?
answer:
There is no cure once a plant breaks with the virus. The control points are planting resistant varieties, avoiding mixing infected material with healthy seed and planting material, and removing affected leaves before they go to seed. There is no spray that reverses this on its own.

What does not change: your timing for clean planting material matters more than almost anything.
